title: "Shall I Pick Them Up, or String Them?"

paragraphs: "Sir! Only now has my writing gained this much influence. I began writing many years ago. My first book was Kizhavan Kanavu. Its price was only three annas. We printed Murasoli leaflets, distributed them free, spoke of our principles through them, and along with that I introduced myself as a writer. Many of today's talented writers are people who advanced only after struggling as I did. Is it fair that you should wish to leap suddenly to the summit?"

I sometimes speak even a little harshly like this to impatient writers who come to see me. I moved forward only step by step. Even now, when I think of it, I feel both happiness and pride at how many hardships we endured in order to become writers.
And I was a writer swimming against the current of society! More frightening still, I was a writer who did not hesitate to point out shortcomings in the Dravidar Kazhagam in which I worked.

Here is a Murasoli leaflet I wrote thirty years ago. A "Varnashrama Conference" was to be held at Chidambaram. This leaflet was printed and distributed on 5 October 1944 in fierce condemnation of it. I reproduce it exactly. Read it.
Murasoli. Origin: E. V. R. Year 67. Drum: 2 — Sound: 7. 1944, Purattasi 20. Writer: Cheran. Secretary: Thennan.
VARNA—OR HONOUR?

At Thillai! Yes—in the fortress of the Dikshitars! In that city of art where, amid resounding music, the Lord lifted his leg and danced before Kali—there is to be a conference of the holy! A feast of religious merit! A gathering of piety! What good can exist so long as fools remain?

At a time when the Congress grudgingly says, "Untouchability must go," when Self-Respecters make the trumpet-call of equality pierce the ears of the Sanatanis, when lions have set out singing, "If anything is called elevation, it is the life of true Tamils," to destroy a life swollen with conceit—there are still perversions in this country that convene a Varnashrama Conference. We must pay attention to the danger that is coming.

These lofty thinkers who lie about at home after eating their fill gathered and devised a way to make a living by dividing people into Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Sudra. This is not merely what I say. It is a truth the country knows, with evidence proclaimed by history.

The intoxicant of "Sudrahood", poured out in the vessel of religion, became a drug that brought stupor into the life of the valiant Tamil. The Dravidian comrade, once intoxicated, has now awakened. He has seen the chapter in which valour was sold and has leapt up in shame. Its echo is the Self-Respect Movement! The Tamil has entered a new epoch—the epoch of Periyar! And he has begun to ask: is the net to be cast once more over such a Tamil's life?

So long as there remain a few "progressives" who believe that attaching tails such as Pillai, Mudaliar, Reddiar and Desikar to their names is the summit of refined living, even our tongue feels a little ashamed when we condemn the fourfold varna. We have no work with savages who say, "Being called a fool suits me; that itself is my title of 'Sir'!" Yet does not pity arise naturally?

They have discovered that only by producing simpletons can they keep themselves merry. And so they sprinkle water over the dead corpse of Varnashrama, call its death a swoon, and shed tears over it. That spectacle is to be staged in Chidambaram on October 8, 9 and 10.

At Thillai a grave will be dug for this attempt to dress the corpse as a bridegroom and extract money from the people. Let all gather and go to wash away the filth! There is no time now merely to sing refrains blaming the enemy. Hurry to Thillai with the metre of liberation!

In the ancient Tamil land that lived with dignity singing many a parani, even if a few selfish brothers with not a shred of shame gather and perform contortions in the hope of establishing varna, at the summit of death itself—O valiant Tamil, fight to guard honour! Down with Varnashrama!

Murasoli, which began in this fashion, is today one of the weapons carried by the soldiers of the liberation army. And I am the Karunanidhi who began writing in this fashion. Should young writers not know the history of how I became a writer? That is why I tell all this.

I cannot think of how I prepared myself for public speaking without recalling my first speech in the school debating contests. The first voice I ever raised standing before an association was on the subject of "Friendship". I spoke with quotations from the Bharatham.

Karna and Duryodhana were intimate friends. One day Karna and Duryodhana's wife were playing chess. At that moment Duryodhana arrived. Seeing her husband come, the wife rose from the game out of respect. Karna, who had not noticed Duryodhana, thought she was trying to leave the game, and pulled at her pearl necklace. The string broke and the pearls scattered to the floor.

Without the slightest suspicion, Duryodhana smiled, patted his friend, and asked: "Shall I pick them up, or string them?" He was asking whether he should gather the scattered pearls and string them again. Karna overflowed at the greatness of his friend's heart. For that friend he later met and opposed his own brothers on the battlefield and finally gave his life.

I narrated this episode beautifully from Villiputhurar's Bharatham and won tremendous support from the assembly. Even the teachers praised me for pouring out a rain of words in beautiful Tamil without stumbling. How were they to know the secret—that for three days and nights I had written the speech, memorized it, and delivered it to the pillars in our house?

Only now do I understand! Karna and Duryodhana possessed that noble quality called friendship—but Karna also had a deeply improper quality in grabbing and pulling the necklace from another man's wife's neck!

I had many close friends whose very presence stirred the heart and encouraged me to speak emotionally about friendship. In this vast world, the greatest wealth I have gained is my friends. Wealth is not gold coins piled up by the crores. The treasure that cannot be found even after searching and searching is a true friend. In that respect I am immensely fortunate.

I followed the Kural, "Friendship is not for laughter alone," and received rebuking advice; I had friends who, "like the hand that rushes to cover the body when the garment slips," removed distress. They were fitting companions to my life.
As today, so even then, I trained myself to live surrounded by friends. I proudly say that through my association with them the flag-hoisting for my present political awakening took place.

Today I have the honour of belonging to the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam; but in 1939 I had been president of the Children's Reform Association! The venue was a palm-leaf hut. The place where it grew was a ruined Anjaneya temple.

The membership fee was a quarter anna. After joining, the weekly subscription was one paisa. All the association's aims were based on discipline and hygiene. No one was to touch beedi or cigarettes. No one was to utter bad words even by mistake. One had to study well. Such were the teachings.

Every week there were special meetings. An elder from the street would come and give advice. But people had to come to the meeting! So beforehand we would announce: "Chocolate will be distributed at the end of the meeting." If we gave it at the beginning, would they remain for the meeting? That was why it was distributed only at the end.

Why are you laughing? You are mocking us for showing chocolate and gathering a crowd, are you not? I ask you: if sundal and chickpeas were not distributed every day at the bhajan hall, would anyone come before dawn in the cold month of Margazhi, getting wet with dew, to sing bhajans? If that is the condition of elders and great devotees, need we even ask about youngsters?

Once a notable named Thambayya Pillai attended our weekly special function. We even put up welcome boards and celebrated with pomp. Look at the alliterative flourish even then: "Welcome, welcome, Thambayya who presides!"

A rival organization called the Youth Association arose against ours. The two associations began attacking one another. Thyagarasan—my inseparable friend, stolen away by death while still young—was the leader of that rival association.

Our association's flag was a two-colour flag of red and white. The Youth Association used as its flag the plough-and-farmer emblem of the Democratic Party. The two groups clashed until violent actions began.
One day, while I was bathing at the side of a well, a stone fell on my head. It was a small stone and did not injure me. A piece of paper had been tied to it. I picked it up and read it.

It asked: "Shall we hold an election between the Youth Association and the Children's Reform Association? Whichever of the two association leaders gets the most votes—shall we agree that the other youngsters will obey his command?"

We accepted that challenge. A voter list was prepared and accepted by both associations. We ourselves created new voters. We had no law like today's saying that only those above twenty-one were voters! We decided that only those aged eighteen and below would be voters.

Accordingly about three hundred voters were registered in our constituency. Both sides plunged vigorously into canvassing for votes. Election day drew nearer and nearer. I contested, and on the other side my friend Thyagarasan contested. The campaign went on vigorously from verandah to verandah, shop to shop.
